transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Russia has released American Stephen Hubbard, who was jailed for over four years on charges
of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
U.S. envoy Steve Whitcoff praised Russian President Vladimir Putin for the move during
a meeting in St. Petersburg.
You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian.
You are a humanitarian also, sir.
Hubbard was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison.
Russian prosecutors said he fought with the Ukrainian military after Russia invaded in
February 2022.
The release comes as President Trump advances policies that aid Putin despite the war, including
waving sanctions on Russia.
Israeli security forces detained a group of activists, including an American who's running
for Congress, that were helping Palestinians harvest olives in the occupied West Bank.
NPR's Ruth Sherlock was there.
For almost two hours, the group helped pick olives with Palestinian owners of the Grove,
close to an Israeli settlement.
Then, the Israeli military and police forces arrived and detained almost the entire group.
Landa, a Democrat from New York, posted this video from the bus on the way to the police
station.
Where occupation is a crime under international law, harvesting olives is not a crime under
any dollar.
Landa and some of the Israeli activists have been released.
The other American activists, as well as a Palestinian family, remain in detention.
Israeli lawyers said this is the largest mass detention of activists in the occupied West
Bank in at least a decade.
Ruth Sherlock, NPR News, in the occupied West Bank.
The Supreme Court has rejected a Trump administration appeal seeking to immediately enforce medical
care restrictions for transgender people in prison.
The decision leaves in place lower court orders requiring prison officials to continue providing
treatments like hormone therapy.
The administration had asked to enforce for now a policy halting gender-affirming surgeries,
hormones and social accommodations.
President Trump travels to South Carolina this evening as part of a midterm campaign
swing to boost support for Republican Senator Darlene Graham.
South Carolina Public Radio's Gavin Jackson reports.
Graham hopes Trump will once again help her with the far-right Republican base, which
favored her run-off opponent, Congressman Ralph Norman, in a close August special primary.
Graham has been loyal to Trump ever since he urged her to run for the full term, following
her appointment to the position by the governor, which followed the death of her brother Lindsey
Graham.
But there's a crack in that support for the president, specifically his move to waive sanctions
against Russia.
I think we need to keep the pressure on Russia, because I don't trust Russia, I don't trust
Russia, so I would prefer keeping the pressure on Russia.
Graham faces Democrat Dr. Annie Andrews a pediatrician on November 3.
For NPR News, I'm Gavin Jackson in Clemson, South Carolina.
Major U.S. stock indexes climbed today after strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital
One and other big companies, the S&P 500, added more than half a percent.
This is NPR.
Humanity is losing ground in its fight against climate change, according to the UN.
If all the countries do what they promised to do to curb climate change, the world will
still warm this century by another 2.2 degrees.
That's about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit warmer than last year's projection.
The UN says much of that is due to the U.S. abandoning its climate efforts.
A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for deceiving users about privacy.
As NPR's Bobby Allen reports, the state says it's one of the largest-ever verdicts against
a tech giant.
The jury found Meta was responsible for violating New Mexico consumer protection laws after
misleading users about its handling of a third-party app connected to the 2018 Cambridge Analytica
data breach, when a consulting firm data mined tens of millions of Facebook users without
their consent.
New Mexico sued the tech giant, saying the company had misrepresented just how safe users'
data was on its social media platforms.
State authorities argued that Meta was liable for tens of millions of violations of the
law, and each penalty carried a fine of $5,000, which is how the judge in the case ordered
Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion.
Meta did not return a request for comment, but has vowed to appeal.
The case harkens back to an era when tech controversies were dominated by fights over
data harvesting, not AI.
Bobby Allen, NPR News.
South Korean officials have freed a large gray shark trapped for over a month in a canal in
Busan.
While experts were concerned about its health due to lack of feeding and falling water temperatures,
they used a floating platform to guide the three-meter-long dusky shark nickname Bukangi
to the sea.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Russia releases American Stephen Hubbard, jailed over four years for fighting as mercenary in Ukraine
Israeli forces detain activists, including American congressional candidate Landa, helping Palestinians harvest olives in West Bank
Supreme Court rejects Trump administration appeal to enforce restrictions on transgender prisoners' medical care
Trump travels to South Carolina to campaign for Senator Darlene Graham ahead of midterms
U.S. stock indexes climb after strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One and other companies
UN says humanity is losing ground on climate change, partly due to U.S. abandoning climate efforts
New Mexico judge orders Meta to pay $25 billion over misleading users about privacy
South Korea frees trapped dusky shark Bukangi from Busan canal back to the sea
